title: Trenette al pesto
subtitle: Ligurian flat pasta with basil pesto, green beans, and potato
excerpt: Trenette al pesto is the Ligurian version of pesto pasta, traditionally served with small pieces of green bean and potato cooked in the same pot as the pasta. The potato thickens the sauce slightly as it collapses, and the beans add a fresh bite. This is how the dish is made in Genoa.
sourceNotes: Ligurian traditional recipe. The combination of pasta, potato, and green beans in one pot with pesto alla genovese is a defining feature of Ligurian cooking. Method drawn from Anna Del Conte, Gastronomy of Italy (2001), and traditional Ligurian cooking sources.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pesto can be made a day ahead and covered with a thin layer of olive oil to prevent browning.

glossaryTerms.definition: The classic basil sauce of Genoa: fresh basil leaves, garlic, pine nuts, Parmesan, Pecorino, and olive oil pounded or blended together.
A flat, slightly narrower pasta ribbon from Liguria, traditionally paired with pesto; similar to linguine but with a rougher, thicker surface.

content.text: Trenette al pesto is the full Ligurian treatment of pesto pasta:
cooked in the same pot as diced potato and green beans. The potato softens and clings to the pasta; the beans add colour and bite; the
pulls everything together at the end. This is the dish as Genoa makes it, not a bowl of spaghetti with basil sauce.

Authentic pesto uses pine nuts, but the ingredient lookup does not carry them; the basil, cheese, oil, and garlic provide the essential character. For the pasta, trenette is sold in Italian delis; linguine is a fine substitute.

Put the basil, {{garlic}} of garlic, {{parmesan}} of Parmesan, {{pecorino-romano}} of Pecorino, and a pinch of salt into a food processor. Pulse until the basil is finely chopped. With the motor running, pour in {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of extra-virgin olive oil in a slow stream. The pesto should be bright green and slightly textured, not a smooth paste. Taste and adjust salt.
Cook the pasta, potato, and beans together

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Add the diced potato and cook for 4 minutes. Add the green beans and cook for 2 minutes more. Add {{pasta-dried}} of trenette and cook until the pasta is al dente, following the packet time. The potato should be tender but not falling apart.
Reserve a mug of pasta water. Drain everything through a colander. Tip into a large warm bowl, spoon the pesto over, and toss well, adding a splash of pasta water to loosen. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Heat or oxidation. Pesto browns if added to the pasta while it is still very hot.
items.fix: Let the drained pasta sit for 30 seconds before adding the pesto. Work quickly and serve immediately.

items.cause: Added too late in the cooking sequence.
items.fix: Always add the potato first, 4 minutes before the pasta, so it has enough time to soften.

items.symptom: Pesto is too thick to toss
items.fix: Add pasta water a tablespoon at a time and toss until the pesto coats the pasta in a fluid film.

content.text: Pesto comes from Genoa and is closely tied to Ligurian cooking. The combination with potato and green beans is how it is eaten in Liguria, though most of the world has never heard of the addition. The potato absorbs the olive oil from the pesto as it softens, giving the dish a richness that pasta alone cannot match.
